clinicalPearls: Severe type I (hypoplasminogenaemic) deficiency causes ligneous, woody, fibrin-rich pseudomembranes on mucous surfaces, most classically the conjunctiva
Pseudomembranes can also affect the gingiva, respiratory tract, middle ear, female genital tract, and rarely the ventricular system, causing occlusive hydrocephalus
Minor mucosal trauma or infection typically triggers membrane formation, which recurs after simple excision
Type I deficiency reduces both plasminogen activity and antigen, whereas type II (dysplasminogenaemia) lowers activity with preserved antigen and is usually asymptomatic
The disorder is one of defective extravascular fibrinolysis rather than a classic bleeding or thrombotic diathesis
Systemic venous thrombosis is not a consistent feature, distinguishing it from the coagulation-cascade thrombophilias
Directed therapy centres on plasma-derived plasminogen replacement together with control of local triggers, with topical measures for ocular disease
reference.pathophysiology: Plasminogen is the zymogen of plasmin, the principal enzyme of fibrinolysis. In severe deficiency, insufficient plasmin activity means fibrin deposited at sites of minor mucosal injury or inflammation cannot be cleared, so it accumulates as firm, woody pseudomembranes rich in fibrin. The defect is one of extravascular fibrin clearance on wet epithelial surfaces, which explains why the eyes, gums, airway and other mucous membranes are affected while systemic thrombosis is uncommon. Biallelic PLG variants underlie the type I phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Cicatricial pemphigoid and other autoimmune conjunctival scarring disorders
Chemical or thermal ocular injury with membrane formation
Congenital hydrocephalus of other cause when ventricular involvement occurs
Chronic gingival hyperplasia from other systemic disease
additionalInvestigations: Plasminogen activity assay and plasminogen antigen to distinguish type I from type II deficiency
Histology of pseudomembranes showing fibrin-rich amorphous material
PLG gene analysis to confirm the diagnosis and support family counselling
Ophthalmic slit-lamp assessment to characterise conjunctival involvement
Imaging of the airway or central nervous system when respiratory or ventricular disease is suspected
Screening for associated infection or inflammation that may trigger membranes
redFlags: Ventricular or intracranial involvement causing occlusive hydrocephalus
Rapidly recurring membranes after surgical removal
Progressive corneal or visual compromise from severe ocular disease
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and relapsing, and untreated mucosal disease can threaten vision or, rarely, the airway and central nervous system. Plasminogen replacement can markedly improve mucosal lesions, so prognosis has improved where such therapy is available.
pitfalls: Repeatedly excising conjunctival membranes without addressing the underlying fibrinolytic defect, leading to recurrence
Confusing asymptomatic type II dysplasminogenaemia with clinically significant type I deficiency
Missing extraocular sites such as the airway or genital tract
Attributing recurrent membranes solely to infection and overlooking the inherited cause
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
management: Provide plasminogen replacement with human plasma-derived plasminogen concentrate as the definitive disease-specific therapy for mucosal pseudomembranes
Treat conjunctival disease with topical plasminogen or fresh frozen plasma eye drops, supplemented by topical heparin, ciclosporin or corticosteroid to limit fibrin deposition
Minimise mucosal trauma and avoid unnecessary surgical excision of membranes, which reliably provokes recurrence
Promptly treat intercurrent infection or inflammation that triggers new membrane formation
Provide multidisciplinary surveillance with ophthalmology for the eyes and monitoring of the airway, ears and genital tract for occlusive disease
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given the autosomal recessive, biallelic PLG inheritance
Escalate urgently for airway obstruction, occlusive hydrocephalus or other sight- or life-threatening involvement
